terms.grammar: the genitive of animus, beside the noun it describes, often set against corporis
evidence: Cic. Fam. 7.1.1: et sine dolōre corporis tē fuisse et animō valuisse
Cic. Fin. 1.59 (Lewis & Short): animī morbī sunt cupiditātēs immēnsae et inānēs
terms.comment: Classical Latin has no adjective for “mental”: it says “of the mind”, animī (animī dolor, mental pain; animī morbus, mental illness, in Cicero a vice or passion), or uses the ablative animō for “mentally” (animō valēre), against corpore, physically.
Where the reason is meant rather than feeling: mentis compos, in one’s right mind (Traupman 155, compos mentis).
Found only once, in a late sermon falsely ascribed to Augustine (Lewis & Short); the classical way is the genitive animī or mentis.

phrases.latin: utrumque laetor, et sine dolōre corporis tē fuisse et animō valuisse
phrases.english: I’m glad of both: that you were free of bodily pain, and that you were mentally sound

phrases.latin: animī valentēs morbō tentārī nōn possunt, corpora possunt
phrases.english: healthy minds cannot be attacked by disease; bodies can
